metadata.title: The Demand Signal Underneath Tesla Stock's Cash-Burn Debate

content.text:
The top line has swung from shrinking to double-digit growth, and one demand driver management points to is the self-driving software already in its cars, not the robots it is building for later.
Tesla (TSLA) has fallen about 21.5% over the past three months and now trades at roughly 71% of its 52-week high. The case against it is easy to state: free cash flow that went negative in Q2 2026 as management had guided, a capital budget that keeps climbing, and a recall covering about 3 million vehicles in China, alongside voluntary recalls from eight other automakers there. Underneath all of that, the revenue line has been going the other way.
Revenue Growth Turned From Negative To 25.5% In Two Quarters
Year-over-year revenue growth ran 11.6%, then -3.1%, then 15.8%, and 25.5% in the most recent quarter. Across the trailing four quarters, that is 11.8%, against a pace of -2.7% in the four quarters before. Two consecutive steps up out of a negative print make a direction, even allowing for the softer year-ago base, and that direction appeared during a twelve-month stretch in which the stock returned -0.2% while the S&P 500 returned 20.3%.
Self-Driving Software Is One Of The Main Reasons Customers Look At The Car
The driver is the software, not the robots. In Q2 2026 about 55% of deliveries in North America had an FSD subscription enabled at the time of delivery, and paid FSD customers reached nearly 1.5 million globally, up from nearly 1.3 million a quarter earlier. By management's own account, the sales data suggests FSD is one of the main reasons customers look at the car. The Model Y set records in several key markets, including the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand, and the company left Q2 2026 with its largest order backlog since 2023. None of that demand story is Optimus, whose early production ramp management he describes as flat and long.
Most Of Q2's Automotive Margin Drop Was A Benefit That Did Not Repeat
Automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits fell sequentially from 19.2% to 16.3% in Q2 2026. Q1 2026 carried about $230 million of warranty true-downs plus some tariff relief that did not repeat, and controlling for those, management says the margin would have been approximately flat. The longer arc is less forgiving: operating margin over the last twelve months was 4.6%, down from 6.2% a year earlier. Management attributed the negative free cash flow mainly to capital spending more than doubling sequentially, and the 2026 budget runs above $25 billion against $103.6 billion of revenue over the trailing twelve months, with the company securing facilities giving it the capacity to borrow up to $30 billion. Tesla is making that bet from a net cash position of about $27.4 billion, more cash on hand than total debt. Defensible balance sheets of that kind are a shared trait of the businesses the Trefis High Quality Portfolio holds.
